statement: In equal circles angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
heath_proof: Let ABC, DEF be equal circles, and let the angles BGC, EHF be angles at their centres G, H, and the angles BAC, EDF angles at the circumferences; I say that, as the circumference BC is to the circumference EF, so is the angle BGC to the angle EHF, and the angle BAC to the angle EDF. For let any number of consecutive circumferences CK, KL be made equal to the circumference BC, and any number of consecutive circumferences FM, MN equal to the circumference EF; and let GK, GL, HM, HN be joined. Then, since the circumferences BC, CK, KL are equal to one another, the angles BGC, CGK, KGL are also equal to one another; [III. 27] therefore, whatever multiple the circumference BL is of BC, that multiple also is the angle BGL of the angle BGC. For the same reason also, whatever multiple the circumference NE is of EF, that multiple also is the angle NHE of the angle EHF. If then the circumference BL is equal to the circumference EN, the angle BGL is also equal to the angle EHN; [III. 27] if the circumference BL is greater than the circumference EN, the angle BGL is also greater than the angle EHN; and, if less, less. There being then four magnitudes, two circumferences BC, EF, and two angles BGC, EHF, there have been taken, of the circumference BC and the angle BGC equimultiples, namely the circumference BL and the angle BGL, and of the circumference EF and the angle EHF equimultiples, namely the circumference EN and the angle EHN. And it has been proved that, if the circumference BL is in excess of the circumference EN, the angle BGL is also in excess of the angle EHN; if equal, equal; and if less, less. Therefore, as the circumference BC is to EF, so is the angle BGC to the angle EHF. [V. Def. 5] But, as the angle BGC is to the angle EHF, so is the angle BAC to the angle EDF; for they are doubles respectively. Therefore also, as the circumference BC is to the circumference EF, so is the angle BGC to the angle EHF, and the angle BAC to the angle EDF.

6.33
**Statement:** In equal circles angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**Step 1.** Let there be equal circles with centres G and H respectively, and let angles BGC and EHF be angles at the centres standing on circumferences BC and EF, and let angles BAC and EDF be angles at the circumferences standing on the same circumferences BC and EF respectively.

**Step 2.** I say that as circumference BC is to circumference EF, so is angle BGC to angle EHF, and also angle BAC to angle EDF.

**Step 3.** Starting from B along the circumference of the first circle, place any number of consecutive arcs CK, KL each equal to circumference BC; and starting from E along the circumference of the second circle, place any number of consecutive arcs FM, MN each equal to circumference EF. Let m arcs equal to BC be placed (so circumference BL is the sum of m arcs each equal to BC), and let n arcs equal to EF be placed (so circumference EN is the sum of n arcs each equal to EF).

**Step 4.** Join GK and GL in the first circle, and HM and HN in the second circle. Since arcs BC, CK, and KL are all equal to one another, the central angles BGC, CGK, and KGL are also equal to one another, by Proposition 3.27 (in equal circles — here in the same circle, which is equal to itself — angles standing on equal circumferences are equal). Therefore angle BGL, which is the sum of m equal angles each equal to angle BGC, is the same multiple of angle BGC that circumference BL is of circumference BC.

**Step 5.** Similarly, angle EHN, which is the sum of n equal angles each equal to angle EHF, is the same multiple of angle EHF that circumference EN is of circumference EF.

**Step 6.** Now if circumference BL is equal to circumference EN, then the arcs BL and EN in the two equal circles are equal, so by Proposition 3.27, angle BGL equals angle EHN.

**Step 7.** If circumference BL is greater than circumference EN, then since BL is a larger arc in a circle equal to the circle containing EN, the angle BGL standing at the centre on BL is greater than angle EHN standing at the centre on EN. For if BGL were not greater, it would be either equal or less. If equal, then by Proposition 3.26 applied inversely — since in equal circles equal central angles stand on equal arcs (3.26 together with 3.27) — arcs BL and EN would be equal, contradicting BL being greater. If BGL were less than EHN, then by the same reasoning EN would be greater than BL, again a contradiction. Therefore angle BGL is greater than angle EHN.

**Step 8.** Similarly, if circumference BL is less than circumference EN, then angle BGL is less than angle EHN.

**Step 9.** Thus we have established: for any equimultiples m of circumference BC and angle BGC, and any equimultiples n of circumference EF and angle EHF, the multiple m times circumference BC exceeds, equals, or falls short of n times circumference EF according as m times angle BGC exceeds, equals, or falls short of n times angle EHF. Therefore by the definition of proportion (Definition 5.5), circumference BC is to circumference EF as angle BGC is to angle EHF.

**Step 10.** Now by Proposition 3.20, angle BGC is double angle BAC, and angle EHF is double angle EDF, since the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference when they stand on the same arc.

**Step 11.** Since angle BGC is to angle EHF as circumference BC is to circumference EF (proved above), and angle BGC is double angle BAC while angle EHF is double angle EDF, by Proposition 5.15 (parts have the same ratio as the same multiples of them), angle BAC is to angle EDF as angle BGC is to angle EHF.

**Step 12.** Therefore angle BAC is to angle EDF as circumference BC is to circumference EF, by Common Notion 1 applied to ratios (i.e., things equal to the same ratio are the same ratio, which is Proposition 5.11).

**Step 13.** Therefore in equal circles, angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences. Q.E.D.
